scope.geographic_emphasis: Primarily Western academic historiography, with selected independent and critical traditions.
notes: Dates describe approximate emergence or expansion, not termination.
Edges are selective teaching interpretations, not an exhaustive genealogy.
Connections may express influence, overlap, conceptual resources, or critique; read each relationship label.
A node’s source is a supporting reference and does not necessarily document every associated edge.
Nodes include traditions, fields, genres, methods, approaches, and individual thinkers.
New and revised relationships may include source_ids and evidence_note. A comparative teaching link does not assert influence merely because it has a source and target.
Editorial revision 1.3 incorporates selected and rewritten Fable 5.1 proposals into the existing revision 1.2; the supplied feedback used an older base and its edge IDs were remapped.

Schema 1.2 adds optional edge directed and relationship_kind fields. Explicit comparisons have directed:false; missing direction metadata on inherited edges means not yet classified, not verified influence. Critique arrows point from critic to the position criticized.

Optional source citation and verification fields distinguish bibliographic identity or supporting-page checks from an unperformed passage-level audit. Missing verification metadata means unrecorded, never implicitly verified. Checked metadata does not certify all node or edge interpretations.

The map remains selective: a named work, school, or field does not imply that every associated thinker agrees. Paired nodes such as Progressive/consensus history are comparisons, not single paradigms.

Revision 1.4 distinguishes women as producers of historical knowledge from women’s history as a field. Women historians appear across economic, political, military, intellectual, and other inquiries; belonging to the profession does not imply a shared feminist method or a linear succession of feminist waves.

Schema 1.3 adds shared people records, explicit group/person entry kinds, and qualified representative_people rosters. Roster inclusion is not a new influence edge or a claim of formal school membership. Most rosters normalize existing curated prose; their inherited references are not new individual affiliation verification.

Directional neighborhood views place incoming directed relationships on the left and outgoing ones on the right. Comparisons and unclassified links sit separately. Thompson’s cultural contribution and feminist historians’ productive inheritance coexist with their criticisms; no uniform succession from class to culture is implied.

From revision 1.133 the atlas has no closing date. Fields are extended one at a time; each entry states the year through which it has been reviewed. The original 1920–2000 experiment (revision 1.121) is kept as an archived view.

frame.note: Open frame from revision 1.133. Each entry records how far it has been reviewed (coverage.reviewed_through); a review year is a limit of our reading, not an ending.

revision_history.summary: Post-2000 wave 2. Four person entries built under the 1920–2000 frame gain their later careers and fuller cores, with read evidence. Joan Wallach Scott gains Davis's acknowledged influence, her use of psychoanalysis and fantasy, her French-feminism and parity books (through Landes and Dean), the veil and secularism books as a contribution to postcolonial critique (through Laborde and Whitney), Laura Lee Downs's 1993 critique, her 2000 reply on class, her 2012 critique of psychohistory and the 2018 Theses on Theory and History. Roger Chartier gains his 1993 questions to Hayden White and White's 1995 rejoinder, his 2003 reassessment of the new cultural history (against reducing practice to discourse; doubting Hunt's coherence), Bourdieu and Certeau as named resources, his Collège de France chair (2007–2016) and his later studies of the mobility of texts. Eric Hobsbawm gains his 1993 Budapest lecture against national myth-making, the Age of… synthesis and Tony Judt's critique of The Age of Extremes, his economic-history core, and dated later books and readings to Evans's 2019 biography. Hayden White gains Paul's 2019 assessment of his place in philosophy of history and the philosophers' criticisms Paul reports, his intellectual-history work, his Holocaust emplotment essay, Cronon's use and dispute, and the practical past. Each ends with at least 10 edges and at least 20 dated points; unread books are attributed to named readers.

events.label: Clausewitz, On War, posthumous publication
events.support: Existing source and Marie von Clausewitz's 1832 preface. Later Graham/Maude edition and apparatus remain distinct; no full German collation.

events.label: Howard, The Franco-Prussian War
events.support: Existing selected reading of Strachan's 2022 memoir, printed pp. 228–231; a retrospective source for the 1961 book.

events.label: Keegan, The Face of Battle
events.support: Existing original-date cross-check; the consulted reprint is 1983 and acknowledgments are dated 1974.

events.label: Bourke, Dismembering the Male
events.support: Existing bibliographic/publisher evidence; a further selected field intervention, not closure of military historiography.

events.label: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War (1.22, 5.68)
events.support: Placed only in the fifth century BCE: a contemporary narrator of the war who says he relied on what he saw and on tested reports (1.22) and recounts the battle of Mantinea, 418 BCE (5.68). The passages read do not date the composition, which may have continued after 401 BCE; ‘approximate’ marks that. A precursor of the genre, not the field’s beginning.

events.label: Polybius, Histories (12.25e–28a; 3.33, 3.48)
events.support: Placed only in the second century BCE: he consulted Hannibal’s own bronze tablet and questioned men present at the Alpine crossing (3.33, 3.48), writing in the generation after Hannibal’s war. No composition year is established by the passages read. A precursor, not a lineage.

events.label: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander, preface
events.support: Placed only in the second century CE: Kromayer and Veith (1928, p. 14) date Arrian’s Tactica to 136/7 CE; the Anabasis itself is not dated in the reading. A precursor, not a lineage.

events.label: Oman, A History of the Art of War: The Middle Ages
events.support: Methuen, 1898; preface signed Oxford, 1 March 1898 (read in full).

events.label: Fortescue, A History of the British Army, vols. I–II
events.support: Macmillan, 1899; preface read in full as reprinted in the 1910 second edition.

events.label: Kromayer’s expedition to Greek battlefields (spring 1900)
events.support: Expedition of spring 1900 with Oberst Janke and a General Staff officer, as Kromayer’s 1903 Vorwort reports; the basis of the 1903 volume, kept as context so that fieldwork is not dated as publication.

events.label: Delbrück, Geschichte der Kriegskunst, vol. I, first preface
events.support: First preface signed 4 June 1900 (existing source note). The four-volume sequence to 1920 is dated in the strategic-scholarship entry.

events.label: Grundy, The Great Persian War
events.support: Murray, 1901; preface read in full (surveys of 1892–99 reported there).

events.label: Oman, A History of the Peninsular War, vol. I
events.support: Oxford, 1902; preface read in part.

events.label: Kromayer, Antike Schlachtfelder in Griechenland, vol. I
events.support: Weidmann, 1903; Vorwort signed October 1902; read in part. The 1900 expedition is a separate context event.

events.label: Wilkinson, The University and the Study of War, inaugural lecture
events.support: Delivered 27 November 1909 and printed by the Clarendon Press the same year (title page); pp. 3–14 read in full.

events.label: Delbrück, Numbers in History, London lectures (6–7 October 1913)
events.support: Two lectures at the University of London, 6–7 October 1913, published the same year; pp. 5–23 read in full.

events.label: Fortescue, Military History: Lectures Delivered at Trinity College, Cambridge
events.support: Cambridge, 1914; he was appointed the college’s first lecturer in military history in 1913. Read in part.

events.label: Edmonds, Military Operations, France and Belgium, 1914, vol. I
events.support: Macmillan, 1922; preface signed April 1922 (read in full). The first published volume, not the beginning of the Historical Section or of official history.

events.label: Parker, The Roman Legions
events.support: Clarendon Press, 1928; preface (February 1928) and contents read.

events.label: Kromayer and Veith, Heerwesen und Kriegführung der Griechen und Römer
events.support: Munich, 1928 (Handbuch der Altertumswissenschaft IV.3.2); pp. V–IX, 1–3 and 14–17 read.

events.label: American Military History Foundation incorporated
events.support: The society’s own chronology: papers filed in Washington on 2 June 1933. An institution’s founding, not the beginning of American military history.

events.label: Journal of the American Military History Foundation, first issue
events.support: The society’s chronology dates the first issue 1 April 1937; the journal was published as Military Affairs from spring 1941 (a title change, not a new journal).

events.label: Morison, History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, vol. II
events.support: Little, Brown, 1947; foreword and introduction read in full. Vol. I was not used.

events.label: Hancock and Gowing, British War Economy
events.support: Date as reported by Morgan-Owen and Finch (2022, pp. 66–67); the book itself is unread here.

events.label: Matloff and Snell, Strategic Planning for Coalition Warfare, 1941–1942
events.support: Office of the Chief of Military History, 1953; foreword dated 5 June 1952; front matter read in full.

continuation.basis: The field is older and broader than these selected works; ancient precursors are not its beginning, and no researched universal interval is proposed.

chronology.interpretation: Use dated works with an explicit selective scope. Thucydides, Polybius and Arrian are context: precursors of the genre, placed only by century, not a lineage or the field’s first years. Oman, Fortescue, Delbrück, Grundy and Kromayer (1898–1903) are a selected cluster of modern scholarly work, not a foundation date; Kromayer’s 1900 expedition is context for his 1903 volume. Official and semi-official histories (Edmonds 1922, Morison 1947, Matloff and Snell 1953) and the American society and journal (1933, 1937) are selected later events, not the beginnings of official or American military history. Howard 1961 and Keegan 1976 are contributions to an older field, not its first and last years. Later memoir dates are evidence dates, not new personal interventions by Howard.
retain: Multiple paradigms, colonial/guerrilla limits of Keegan's frame, and collaboration/editorial labour.
Ancient precursors are not a continuous lineage; the modern selection concentrates on British, American and German scholarship.
unresolved: If phase bars are useful, define their subject and geography; do not construct a universal beginning from the oldest source in this selection.
Composition dates of the ancient works were not checked; they are placed by century only. Caesar, Herodotus and Xenophon are discussed only through modern critics and are not dated here.
